prompt:
Formulate a non-aqueous electrolyte for a lithium-ion battery using lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF6) as the salt. The electrolyte composition is 1.2M LiPF6 in a binary solvent of ethylene carbonate (EC) and propylene carbonate (PC) at 1:1 volume ratio. This cell will use a graphite anode and LiCoO2 cathode, operating between 3.0V and 4.2V.

The EC/PC solvent system is chosen because PC has a low melting point (-49°C), enabling operation down to -40°C, while EC provides good ionic conductivity. We have tested the electrolyte conductivity at 25°C and measured 10.5 mS/cm, which we consider adequate. The upper voltage limit of 4.2V is within the electrochemical stability window of the carbonate solvents, which we claim extends to approximately 5.0V vs Li/Li+. Please review the electrolyte formulation and its compatibility with the electrode materials.

seeded_faults.description: Propylene carbonate co-intercalates with lithium ions into graphite anodes, causing exfoliation and destruction of the graphite structure during the first charge cycle. This is a well-established and critical incompatibility in lithium-ion battery chemistry. PC-based electrolytes can only be used with non-graphitisable (hard) carbon anodes or with graphite anodes if the PC content is very low (<20%) and offset by high EC content with effective SEI-forming additives (like vinylene carbonate). The 1:1 EC/PC ratio with a graphite anode will result in catastrophic first-cycle capacity loss and cell failure.
seeded_faults.location_hint: 1:1 EC/PC solvent ratio used with a graphite anode.

seeded_faults.description: The claim that carbonate solvents have an electrochemical stability window extending to 5.0V vs Li/Li+ is misleading. While the oxidative decomposition potential of pure EC/PC measured on inert electrodes (Pt, glassy carbon) is approximately 4.5-5.0V vs Li/Li+, on actual cathode surfaces (LiCoO2, LiMn2O4) catalytic decomposition begins at significantly lower potentials — around 4.3-4.5V vs Li/Li+. At 4.2V cell voltage (which corresponds to approximately 4.2V vs Li/Li+ at the cathode), the system is near the practical stability limit. The stated 5.0V stability window creates false confidence for potential future use at higher voltages and misrepresents the actual margin.
seeded_faults.location_hint: Claim that electrochemical stability window extends to approximately 5.0V vs Li/Li+.

ground_truth_notes: Two faults: (1) PC co-intercalation into graphite is a fundamental incompatibility discovered in early Li-ion research. Fong et al., J. Electrochem. Soc. 137, 2009 (1990). EC forms a stable SEI on graphite; PC does not. The 1:1 EC/PC ratio will destroy the graphite anode. (2) Practical oxidative stability of carbonates on oxide cathode surfaces is 4.3-4.5V vs Li/Li+, not 5.0V. The higher value applies only to inert electrode measurements. Reference: Xu, 'Nonaqueous Liquid Electrolytes for Lithium-Based Rechargeable Batteries', Chemical Reviews, 104, 4303 (2004).
